locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: The Pear Tree

source_text:
PEAR Trees are so well known, that they need no description.

_Government and virtues._] The Tree belongs to Venus, and so doth the
Apple tree. For their physical use they are best discerned by their
taste. All the sweet and luscious sorts, whether manured or wild, do
help to move the belly downwards, more or less. Those that are hard and
sour, do, on the contrary, bind the belly as much, and the leaves do
so also: Those that are moist do in some sort cool, but harsh or wild
sorts much more, and are very good in repelling medicines; and if the
wild sort be boiled with mushrooms, it makes them less dangerous. The
said Pears boiled with a little honey, help much the oppressed stomach,
as all sorts of them do, some more, some less: but the harsher sorts
do more cool and bind, serving well to be bound to green wounds, to
cool and stay the blood, and heal up the green wound without farther
trouble, or inflammation, as Galen saith he hath found by experience.
The wild Pears do sooner close up the lips of green wounds than others.

Schola Selerni advises to drink much wine after Pears, or else (say
they) they are as bad as poison; nay, and they curse the tree for it
too; but if a poor man find his stomach oppressed by eating Pears, it
is but working hard, and it will do as well as drinking wine.

pubmed.title: Pyrus communis L. (Pear) and Malus domestica Borkh. (apple) leaves lipoidal extracts as sources for beta-sitosterol rich formulae and their wound healing evaluation.
pubmed.relevance_note: Evaluates wound healing potential of leaf extracts.

evidence.summary: Modern literature supports antibacterial and wound-healing properties via phenolics and beta-sitosterol, aligning with traditional uses for green wounds. Digestive benefits are implied by general health reviews, though specific 'oppressed stomach' mechanisms require further targeted study.

pubmed.title: Toxic Risks of Nightshade Species: A comprehensive review of the documented toxicity of Atropa belladonna, Solanum dulcamara, and Solanum nigrum.
pubmed.relevance_note: Documents severe toxicity risks for S. dulcamara, contradicting traditional use for internal ailments like stomach casting or swellings.

pubmed.title: Spirosolane-containing Solanum species and induction of congenital craniofacial malformations.
pubmed.relevance_note: Links specific Solanum species to congenital malformations, raising safety concerns for traditional internal applications.

evidence.summary: Modern toxicology confirms high risks of S. dulcamara for internal use (stomach/belly), directly contradicting historical indications for 'vicious humours' or swellings. External use may be safer but requires caution due to alkaloid content.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence shows antibacterial mechanisms (PMID: 40149091) and toxicity risks for Solanum dulcamara (PMID: 41819152), offering limited plausibility for wound cooling or mushroom mitigation, but no clinical support for stomach relief.
concordance.uncertainty: Evidence is preclinical; historical claims lack modern clinical validation.
caveats: No human trials for gastric use
